passage: The hostel emptied out the night before Diwali, trolley bags rattling down the corridor. Sachin's ticket home had waitlisted, and rebooking cost more than he had. His mother called on video while a noisy crowd of leavers passed behind him. "Sab theek hai, ma, everyone's here, big dinner," he said, and hung up smiling. Then he sat in the empty mess, sure that every other person in the building had a crowd. Chandrika from the third floor came in to make instant noodles. She had stayed too. "You look like I felt last week," she said. "Honestly? I've eaten alone since September." Sachin's throat tightened. "Me too," he said at last, and the words felt lighter than the smile he had put on for the call.

qa.q: Why did Sachin stay in the hostel over Diwali?
qa.a: His ticket home had waitlisted and rebooking cost more than he had.

qa.q: Why did Sachin tell his mother that everyone was there for a big dinner?
qa.a: He seems ashamed of being alone and wanted to look fine, and the smile as he hung up suggests he was hiding how he really felt.

qa.q: What might Sachin do after Chandrika's honest words?
qa.a: Sachin could keep talking with Chandrika, perhaps share meals with her, and tell his mother the truth when he is ready.

qa.q: What is it like for Chandrika to say she has eaten alone since September?
qa.a: It may feel like a risk and a relief, because saying it lets Sachin see that he is not the only one.

grounding: Sachin believes everyone else has friends, pretends to be fine to his mother, then has one honest conversation.

passage: Mei told her mother on every call that uni in Melbourne was 'great, so busy'. It wasn't. Five weeks in, she ate lunch on the library steps, watching groups laughing on the lawn, sure that everyone else had found their people in week one. She had even posted a photo of a crowded party she'd walked past, as if she had been inside. In Thursday's tutorial, Yara, who always sat by the door, asked if she wanted to grab a coffee. Mei nearly said she was busy. Then, halfway through the coffee, she said something she hadn't planned: 'Honestly, I don't really know anyone here yet.' Yara put down her cup. 'Me neither. Some days I've eaten lunch in the bathroom.' They both laughed, a little shocked. The next Thursday they sat together, and Mei called her mother and said, 'It's hard, actually.'

qa.a: Mei ate lunch on the library steps.

qa.q: What was Mei feeling as she watched the groups on the lawn?
qa.a: Mei felt lonely and ashamed, sure everyone else had found friends in week one.
Telling Yara honestly that she didn't know anyone, because it let Yara admit the same and turned shame into connection.

qa.q: How does Yara respond to Mei's honesty, and why?
qa.a: Yara seems relieved enough to admit being lonely too, even eating lunch in the bathroom some days.

grounding: Shows the belief that everyone else has friends, the cover-up of pretending, and one honest conversation revealing the feeling is shared.

passage: The notice board in the trainees' common room at the nursing college in Kochi was full of photos: Onam celebrations, group trips, birthday cakes. Neelam wasn't in any of them. Two months in, she smiled in class, answered every question and told everyone she was 'totally settled'. At night she walked the corridor so she wouldn't have to sit alone in her room. One evening the warden's assistant, Sangeeta, found her there at eleven. 'You walk here a lot,' Sangeeta said, not unkindly. Neelam started to say she was fine, and then didn't. 'I think everyone here has friends except me.' Sangeeta sat on the bench. 'I counted once. Half the trainees in this block tell me that in their first term.' Neelam laughed in disbelief. Sangeeta pointed at the board. 'Photos don't show who went home and cried.' The next week, Neelam signed up for the block's Sunday cooking rota.

qa.q: What did the photos on the notice board show?
qa.a: The photos showed Onam celebrations, group trips and birthday cakes.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling while walking the corridor at night?
qa.a: Neelam felt lonely and ashamed, pretending to be settled while believing everyone else had friends.

qa.q: What helped Neelam move past pretending?
qa.a: Admitting the truth to Sangeeta and then joining the Sunday cooking rota.

qa.q: How does Sangeeta see Neelam's loneliness?
qa.a: Sangeeta sees it as very common, hearing the same thing from half the trainees in the block in their first term.

grounding: Shows a trainee pretending to be settled while ashamed of being lonely, and one honest talk showing that many feel the same.
